notes.short: “You neatly set aside”: praise that rebukes
notes.about: Jesus seems to praise the Pharisees and scribes for how neatly they set aside God's command. He means the opposite: they had done evil. The next verses show how: their tradition kept a man from doing anything for his father or mother.

figure.name: Irony
figure.means: that they did evil, not well, in setting aside God's command for their tradition

original.note: In Mark's Greek “neatly” is kalōs, “well”, a word that means suitably or becomingly.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under irony spoken by God, brought out by the word for well, which means suitably: they did evil, not well. Clarke calls the word a strong irony: how noble their conduct, to annul God's commandments for their own traditions.
notes.limit: Not every writer reads irony here: some take the word plainly, as wholly, and others read the words as a question or as praise of their cunning.

cites.at: Eironeia, or Irony: Divine Irony, p. 811
cites.quote: Here the Irony is beautifully brought out by translating καλῶς (kalōs) “full well.”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Full well - Καλως, - a strong irony. How noble is your conduct! From conscientious attachment to your own traditions ye have annihilated the commandments of God!
